## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Alambusājātaka* (Ja 523) is a narrative belonging to the Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral]. Its frame story, set at Jetavana, recounts how the Buddha addressed a monk who had been unsettled by the sight of his former wife; the Buddha explains that in a previous life she had similarly brought about his downfall, causing him to lose his meditative attainments and spend three years in sensual distraction before lamenting and recovering his senses [SuttaCentral]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta's ascetic son Isisinga (the Pali counterpart of the epic figure Ṛṣyaśṛṅga), who was born from a doe that consumed water containing an ascetic's semen, performs such intense tapas that Śakra's throne grows hot and the deity fears losing his celestial sovereignty [Winternitz 1933; Ohnuma 2007; Olson 2015]. To neutralize the threat, Śakra dispatches the celestial nymph (*accharā*) Alambusā to seduce the naive recluse [Ohnuma 2007; Olson 2015; Fausböll 1891]. The inexperienced Isisinga succumbs to her allure and remains captivated for three years, until he awakens to his lapse, renounces lust, forgives Alambusā, and regains his ascetic powers [Ohnuma 2007; Olson 2015].
The tale represents a Buddhist adaptation of the widely distributed ancient Indian motif of the seduction of an innocent ascetic, which shares common heritage with episodes in the *Mahābhārata* and the *Rāmāyaṇa*, as well as the related *Naḷinikājātaka* (Ja 526) [Mylius 2003; Winternitz 1933; Lang 2003; Olson 2015]. Versions of the narrative frame also feature prominently in Buddhist monastic literature, such as the *Mahāsāṅghika-vinaya*, where the monk Nandika is identified with the hermit's child seduced by Alambusā in an earlier life [Clarke, Parajika Penance; Clarke, Pārājika]. The antiquity of the legend is confirmed by early Buddhist art, being depicted in stone reliefs at both Bharhut and Sāñcī [Sarao and Long 2017; Winternitz 1933]. Philologically, the text's verses and commentary highlight the intensity of the ascetic's sudden infatuation, using predatory imagery marked by terms such as *ajjhāpatto* [von Hinüber 1994].
DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal text reuse between Ja 523 and its commentary in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, as well as shared gnomic or narrative verses with other ascetic stories, notably the *Akittijātaka* (Ja 480) and the *Kaṇhajātaka* (Ja 440) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also records cross-linguistic textual alignments with Chinese Āgama and Tibetan canonical texts (such as the *Vinayavibhaṅga* and Aśvaghoṣa's *Buddhacarita*), though these reflect broader formulaic parallels rather than direct textual correspondences [DharmaNexus].
